A skipped stitch happens when the needle thread does not connect with the bobbin thread. The needle carries the upper thread below the needle plate, where a rotating hook should catch it and form a stitch. If the hook misses the thread loop, the machine leaves a gap.

The most common cause is the needle. Replace it with a new needle, even if the old one looks fine. A slightly bent or blunt needle can cause repeated skipping. Make sure it is the correct type and size for the fabric. Use a stretch or ballpoint needle for knits, and a sharp universal or microtex needle for most woven fabrics. Insert it as far as it will go, with the flat side facing the direction stated in the manual.

Incorrect threading is another common cause, especially on a recently purchased machine. Raise the presser foot before threading the upper thread. This opens the tension discs so the thread can enter them properly. Raise the needle to its highest position, then follow every thread guide in the correct order. Make sure the thread passes through the take up lever and through the needle in the correct direction.

Remove and reinstall the bobbin as well. Check that it is wound evenly, fitted in the correct direction, and threaded through the bobbin tension slot. If the machine uses a removable bobbin case, make sure the case is seated firmly. Use the correct bobbin type, since similar looking bobbins are not always interchangeable.

Skipped stitches can also result from unsuitable thread, very thick fabric, stretchy material, or several bulky seams. Try good quality thread and avoid combining a very fine needle with thick thread. Do not pull or push the fabric while sewing, since this can bend the needle away from the hook. Let the feed mechanism move the fabric.

Because the machine is second hand, clean lint and old thread from the bobbin area and around the feed dogs. Unplug the machine before cleaning. Follow the manual for lubrication, since some machines need oil and others should not be oiled by the user.

Test the machine on a folded piece of ordinary cotton using a new universal needle, normal polyester thread, a medium stitch length, and moderate tension. If it still skips after correct threading and bobbin installation, the needle timing may be wrong. This means the hook is not passing the needle at the proper moment. Timing adjustment usually requires a sewing machine technician, particularly if the needle has previously struck the needle plate or a pin.
quality_reasoning: The response fully addresses the task by clearly explaining why a sewing machine skips stitches and covering all major causes (needle, threading, bobbin, fabric, timing) with practical advice tailored to someone who has just bought a second-hand machine.
